The price profiles (Section 2.2) build off of previously developed prices for 2019 that were originally developed based on the CalFUSE framework and then adjusted to be revenue neutral to each class average load shape, as opposed to being universal across customer classes. In this study, we develop price multiple scenarios by adjusting what portion of total electricity costs are allocated “dynamically”, as opposed to being constant in every hour. Further, we forecast electricity costs and total revenue requirements to 2030 and then develop 2030 price profiles based on previously developed forecasts of system net load. Technology cost estimates (Section 2.5) are also included, in order to assess the potential for cost-effective flexibility under different dynamic price scenarios. We use several metrics to quantify the impacts of the price response, including: customer bill impacts, system avoided costs, avoided emissions, effective shed capacity, customer cost- benefit ratio, and payback period. These metrics are further described in Section 2.6. 2.1 Baseline load data The baseline load profiles used in this study come from a dataset of cluster load shapes developed as a part of California Phase 4 Demand Response Potential Study (hereinafter referred to as Phase 4 study) (Gerke et al. 2024). This dataset was developed based on data 6 provided by the three major investor-owned utilities11 in California, namely the demographic information of all service accounts at the time (location, tariff, NAICS code, peak demand, annual energy consumption, etc.) and AMI data for a sample of 3% of customer accounts for the years 2018 and 2019. The resulting AMI dataset comprised over 400,000 customers across residential, commercial, industrial, and agricultural sectors. The customer-level AMI data was cleaned and processed to account for behind-the-meter PV generation, public safety power shutoffs, and other irregularities. Then customers were grouped into clusters, and their demand profiles were weighted (according to sample weights) and aggregated into cluster time series. The clustering process involved a multi-level clustering methodology that segmented customers based on their demographic, geographic, and load consumption characteristics, resulting in 5,422 customer clusters; the sum of which represents the total load served across the three IOUs. The cluster load profiles were then disaggregated across several end uses using various methodologies. Space heating and cooling loads are disaggregated using a temperature normalization model at the individual time series level and aggregated at the cluster level. Water heating, pool pump, and spa pump loads were disaggregated using publicly available Residential Appliance Saturation Survey (RASS) data (Palmgren et al. 2021) and hourly end use load profile (CEC-ADM) datasets (Baroiant et al. 2019). Presence of EVs were determined for each cluster based on a mix of tariffs, rebates, and known number of EVs in each IOU. The saturation of Level 1 and Level 2 charging was determined using the RASS dataset along with the relevant charging load profile from EVI-Pro (NREL 2022).
